edition.name: Migne, Patrologia Latina (PL 2, Paris 1844), De carne Christi, via Latin Wikisource transcription
edition.witness_note: Single locked witness in repo; second witness not yet locked.

source_text: Licuit et Valentino, ex privilegio haeretico, carnem Christi spiritalem comminisci. Quidvis eam fingere potuit, quisquis humanam credere noluit; quando (quod ad omnes dictum est) si humana non fuit, nec ex homine, non video ex qua substantia ipse se, Christus hominem et filium hominis pronuntiarit: Nunc autem vultis occidere hominem veritatem ad vos locutum; et: Dominus est sabbati filius hominis. De ipso enim Esaias: Homo in plaga, et sciens ferre imbecillitatem; et Hieremias: Et homo est, et quis cognoscet illum? et Daniel: Et super nubes tanquam filius hominis. Etiam Paulus apostolus: Mediator Dei et hominum, homo Christus Jesus. Item Petrus in Actis Apostolorum: Jesum Nazarenum, virum vobis a Deo destinatum, utique hominem. Haec sola sufficere vice praescriptionis debuerunt ad testimonium carnis humanae, et ex homine sumptae, et non spiritalis; sicut nec animalis, nec sidereae, nec imaginariae; si sine studio et artificio contentionis haereses esse potuissent. Nam ut penes quemdam ex Valentini factione legi, primo non putant terrenam, et humanam Christo substantiam informatam, ne deterior angelis Dominus deprehendatur, qui non terrenae carnis extiterunt; dehinc, quod oporteret similem nostri carnem similiter nasci, non de spiritu, nec de Deo, sed ex viri voluntate. Et cur non de corruptela, sed de incorruptela? Et quare non, sicut et illa resurrexit, et in coelo resumpta est, ita et nostra, par ejus, statim assumitur? aut cur illa, par nostrae, non aeque in terram dissoluta est? Talia et ethnici volutabunt: Ergo Dei Filius in tantum humilitatis exhaustus? Et, si resurrexit in exemplum spei nostrae, cur nihil tale de nobis probatum est? Merito ethnici talia, sed merito et haeretici. Numquid enim inter illos distat, nisi quod ethnici non credendo credunt, at haeretici credendo non credunt? Legunt denique: Minorasti eum modico citra angelos, et negant inferiorem substantiam Christi; nec hominem se, sed vermem pronuntiantis; qui nec formam habuit, nec speciem; sed forma ejus ignobilis, despecta citra omnes homines; homo in plaga, et sciens ferre imbecillitatem. Agnoscunt hominem Deo mixtum, et negant hominem. Mortuum credunt, et quod est mortuum, ex incorruptela natum esse contendunt: quasi corruptela aliud sit a morte. «Sed et nostra caro statim resurgere debebat.» Exspecta: nondum inimicos suos Christus oppressit, ut cum amicis de inimicis triumphet.
pass_a_gloss: It was also permitted to Valentinus, from the privilege of a heretic, to devise a spiritual flesh of Christ. Anyone who did not want to believe in human flesh could imagine it to be anything; for (as has been said to all) if it was not human, nor from a human being, I do not see from what substance Christ Himself would have called Himself a human being and the son of a human being: Now you want to kill the human being who has spoken the truth to you; and: The Lord of the Sabbath is the son of a human being. For Isaiah says about Him: A human being in a plague, and knowing how to bear weakness; and Jeremiah: And He is a human being, and who will know Him? and Daniel: And on the clouds like the son of a human being. Also, the apostle Paul: The mediator of God and human beings, the human being Christ Jesus. Likewise, Peter in the Acts of the Apostles: Jesus the Nazarene, a man appointed by God for you, certainly a human being. These things alone should have been sufficient as a testimony to the human flesh taken from a human being, and not spiritual; just as it is neither animal nor celestial nor imaginary; if heresies could have existed without the zeal and artifice of contention. For, as I have read from a certain member of Valentinus' faction, at first they do not think that Christ's substance was formed from earthly and human material, lest the Lord be found to be inferior to the angels, who were not made of earthly flesh; then, that it was necessary for Him to be born with flesh similar to ours, not from the Spirit, nor from God, but from the will of a man. And why not from corruption, but from incorruption? And why not, just as that flesh also rose again and was taken up into heaven, so also our flesh, equal to His, is immediately assumed? or why not, just as that flesh, equal to ours, was not equally dissolved into the earth? The Gentiles will also ask such questions: Therefore, the Son of God was exhausted to such an extent of humility? And, if He rose again as an example of our hope, why has nothing similar been proven about us? The Gentiles deserve such questions, but so do the heretics. For what difference is there between them, except that the Gentiles, not believing, believe, while the heretics, believing, do not believe? They read, finally: You have made Him a little lower than the angels, and they deny that Christ's substance is inferior; nor do they call Him a human being, but a worm; who had neither form nor appearance; but His form was ignoble, despised below all human beings; a human being in a plague, and knowing how to bear weakness. They acknowledge a human being mixed with God, and they deny the human being. They believe that He died, and they contend that what is dead was born from incorruption: as if corruption were something other than death. But also our flesh ought to have risen immediately. Wait: Christ has not yet overcome His enemies, so that He may triumph over His enemies with His friends.

pass_b_english: Valentinus, invoking the heretic's privilege, also tried to devise a "spiritual flesh" for Christ. Anyone who refused to believe Christ was truly human could imagine His body to be anything at all. After all, as has been said to everyone: if Christ was not human, and not from a human being, I cannot see from what substance He would have called Himself a human being and the Son of Man. Jesus said, "Now you want to kill me, a man who has told you the truth" (John 8:40), and "The Son of Man is Lord of the Sabbath" (Mark 2:28). Isaiah speaks of Him: "A man of suffering, acquainted with weakness" (Isaiah 53:3). Jeremiah asks: "He is a man, and who can know him?" (Jeremiah 17:9 LXX). Daniel sees "one like a son of man coming with the clouds" (Daniel 7:13). The apostle Paul writes: "The mediator of God and men, the man Christ Jesus" (1 Timothy 2:5). Peter declares in Acts: "Jesus of Nazareth, a man accredited by God to you" (Acts 2:22). These testimonies alone should have been sufficient proof that Christ's flesh was human, taken from a human being — not spiritual, just as it was not animal, celestial, or imaginary — if heresies could exist without the zeal and artifice of contention.

I have read the writings of a certain Valentinian. First, they deny that Christ's substance was formed from earthly, human material, lest the Lord be found inferior to the angels, who were not made of earthly flesh. Then they claim it was necessary for Him to be born with flesh similar to ours, but not from the Spirit, nor from God, but from the will of a man. But why from incorruption rather than corruption? And why, if that flesh rose and was taken up into heaven, is our flesh — equal to His — not immediately assumed? Or why, if that flesh was equal to ours, was it not equally dissolved into the earth? Even pagans raise such objections: "Was the Son of God reduced to such depths of humility?" And: "If He rose as the pattern of our hope, why has nothing similar been proven in us?" Pagans deserve to ask these things, but so do heretics. What difference is there between them, except that pagans, by not believing, believe, while heretics, by believing, do not believe?

Finally, they read: "You made him a little lower than the angels" (Psalm 8:5), yet they deny that Christ's substance is inferior. They refuse to call Him a man, calling Him instead a worm — "who had no form or comeliness" (Isaiah 53:2), "a man of suffering, acquainted with weakness" (Isaiah 53:3). They acknowledge a man mixed with God, yet they deny the man. They believe He died, yet they contend that what is dead was born from incorruption — as if corruption were something other than death. "But our flesh ought to have risen immediately." Wait. Christ has not yet crushed His enemies, so that He may triumph over them together with His friends.

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the Latin text. Scripture citations in Pass B are correctly identified and added (e.g., John 8:40, Mark 2:28, Psalm 8:5, Isaiah 53:3, 1 Timothy 2:5, Acts 2:22) based on the context of the Latin quotes. The distinction between 'corruption' and 'incorruption' is preserved. The nuances of the Valentinian arguments are maintained.
